subtopics.title: main idea and supporting evidence
subtopics.teaching: The main idea is the central point of a passage; supporting evidence includes details, examples, reasons or facts that develop that point.
subtopics.worked_example: If a passage explains how regular reading improves vocabulary and then gives several examples, the vocabulary benefit is the main idea and the examples are supporting evidence.
subtopics.pitfall: A vivid detail is not automatically the main idea.
subtopics.mastery: State the central idea and select details that directly support it.

subtopics.title: inference from explicit clues
subtopics.teaching: An inference is a reasonable conclusion supported by clues in the text rather than a sentence copied directly from it.
subtopics.worked_example: If a character carries an umbrella, wears a raincoat and avoids puddles, rain is a reasonable inference even if the passage never says 'it is raining.'
subtopics.pitfall: An inference must be supported by textual evidence, not personal imagination.
subtopics.mastery: Make inferences by combining explicit clues and rejecting unsupported assumptions.

subtopics.title: sequence cause and effect
subtopics.teaching: Sequence identifies the order of events; cause explains why something happens and effect describes what follows.
subtopics.worked_example: A storm causes a power cut, which then causes a computer to shut down: the storm is an earlier cause and the shutdown is a later effect.
subtopics.pitfall: The first event in a passage is not necessarily the cause of every later event.
subtopics.mastery: Trace chronological order and distinguish causes from consequences.

subtopics.title: author purpose and tone
subtopics.teaching: Author purpose describes why a text was written, such as to inform, explain, persuade or entertain. Tone describes the writer's attitude.
subtopics.worked_example: A notice giving exam timings mainly informs, while an advertisement encouraging readers to buy a product aims to persuade.
subtopics.pitfall: Purpose and tone are related but not identical.
subtopics.mastery: Identify purpose from content and tone from word choice and attitude.

subtopics.title: fact opinion and interpretation
subtopics.teaching: A fact can be checked against evidence; an opinion expresses a judgment or belief; an interpretation explains meaning from available evidence.
subtopics.worked_example: 'The library opens at 9 a.m.' is checkable, while 'The library is the best place in town' is an opinion.
subtopics.pitfall: An opinion can sound confident without becoming a fact.
subtopics.mastery: Classify statements and justify the classification from the wording and evidence.

subtopics.title: context clues
subtopics.teaching: Context clues are nearby words or sentences that help determine an unfamiliar word's meaning.
subtopics.worked_example: In 'The glass was fragile, so it broke when dropped,' the consequence supplies a clue that fragile means easily broken.
subtopics.pitfall: Choosing the most familiar dictionary meaning can be wrong when context points to another sense.
subtopics.mastery: Infer word meaning using surrounding evidence before selecting an option.

subtopics.title: synonyms and antonyms
subtopics.teaching: Synonyms have similar meanings and antonyms have contrasting meanings, but the relationship depends on context and part of speech.
subtopics.worked_example: 'Rapid' and 'swift' are close synonyms when describing movement; 'rapid' and 'slow' are contrasts.
subtopics.pitfall: Words that look related are not necessarily interchangeable in every sentence.
subtopics.mastery: Select a synonym or antonym that fits both meaning and grammatical use.

subtopics.title: word families
subtopics.teaching: A word family contains related forms built around a common base, often changing part of speech or grammatical function.
subtopics.worked_example: Decide, decision and decisive share a base idea but serve different grammatical roles.
subtopics.pitfall: Related words can differ in meaning enough that replacing one with another changes the sentence.
subtopics.mastery: Use word-family relationships to infer meaning and choose the correct form.

subtopics.title: roots prefixes and suffixes
subtopics.teaching: Roots carry core meaning while prefixes and suffixes modify meaning or grammatical role.
subtopics.worked_example: 'Un-' can reverse meaning in words such as unhappy; '-less' can indicate absence, as in careless.
subtopics.pitfall: A prefix or suffix does not always give a complete definition without context.
subtopics.mastery: Break unfamiliar words into meaningful parts and test the resulting meaning against context.

subtopics.title: precision in word choice
subtopics.teaching: Precise word choice selects the word that conveys the intended meaning, strength and tone most accurately.
subtopics.worked_example: 'Stroll' suggests a relaxed walk, while 'march' suggests purposeful movement; both relate to walking but are not interchangeable.
subtopics.pitfall: Using a broad synonym can remove an important distinction.
subtopics.mastery: Choose vocabulary based on meaning, context, intensity and tone.

subtopics.title: parts of speech
subtopics.teaching: Parts of speech describe grammatical roles such as noun, verb, adjective, adverb, pronoun, preposition and conjunction.
subtopics.worked_example: In 'The bright bird flew quickly,' bird is a noun, bright an adjective, flew a verb and quickly an adverb.
subtopics.pitfall: A word's part of speech can depend on how it functions in a sentence.
subtopics.mastery: Identify words by their function in the sentence, not by memorized appearance alone.

subtopics.title: sentence structure
subtopics.teaching: A complete sentence normally expresses a complete thought and contains an appropriate subject and predicate; clauses can be independent or dependent.
subtopics.worked_example: 'Because the rain stopped' is dependent and incomplete by itself, while 'The match resumed' is an independent clause.
subtopics.pitfall: Adding a capital letter and full stop does not turn a fragment into a complete sentence.
subtopics.mastery: Identify sentence boundaries and distinguish complete clauses from fragments.

subtopics.title: subject verb agreement
subtopics.teaching: The finite verb must agree with its subject in number and person.
subtopics.worked_example: 'The list of names is on the desk' uses is because list, not names, is the subject.
subtopics.pitfall: A nearby plural noun can distract from the true singular subject.
subtopics.mastery: Locate the grammatical subject before choosing the verb form.

subtopics.title: verb tenses
subtopics.teaching: Verb tense locates an action in time and can show relationships between events.
subtopics.worked_example: 'She finished the work before the teacher arrived' uses past forms to show two completed events, with before establishing their order.
subtopics.pitfall: Changing tense without a reason can make time relationships unclear.
subtopics.mastery: Choose tense from the intended time reference and relationship between actions.

subtopics.title: pronouns and modifiers
subtopics.teaching: Pronouns replace nouns; modifiers describe or limit words. Both should have clear references and logical placement.
subtopics.worked_example: In 'After reading the book, Maya wrote a review,' Maya is the person who read the book, so the modifier is logically attached.
subtopics.pitfall: A misplaced modifier can accidentally suggest that the wrong subject performed an action.
subtopics.mastery: Use clear pronoun references and place modifiers next to the words they logically describe.

subtopics.title: punctuation
subtopics.teaching: Punctuation marks clarify sentence boundaries, pauses, relationships and meaning.
subtopics.worked_example: 'Let's eat, Grandma' uses a comma to address Grandma; removing it changes the reading.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not insert commas merely wherever speech pauses.
subtopics.mastery: Choose punctuation from grammatical structure and intended meaning.

subtopics.title: capitalization
subtopics.teaching: Capital letters begin sentences and proper nouns and appear in established uses such as titles and the pronoun I.
subtopics.worked_example: 'Monday' is capitalized because it names a day, while 'month' is normally lowercase generically.
subtopics.pitfall: Capitalizing a common noun does not make it a proper noun.
subtopics.mastery: Apply capitalization rules consistently.

subtopics.title: common usage errors
subtopics.teaching: Common errors include agreement, homophones, tense consistency and faulty pronoun reference.
subtopics.worked_example: 'Their going to school' should be 'They're going to school'; their is possessive.
subtopics.pitfall: A word can sound right while being grammatically wrong.
subtopics.mastery: Identify the error and explain the context-appropriate correction.

subtopics.title: sentence correction
subtopics.teaching: Sentence correction checks grammar, meaning, agreement, tense, word choice and completeness.
subtopics.worked_example: 'Neither the teacher nor the students were ready' uses agreement with the nearer plural subject.
subtopics.pitfall: A correction that changes intended meaning is not successful.
subtopics.mastery: Make the smallest accurate correction while preserving meaning.

subtopics.title: passage editing
subtopics.teaching: Passage editing checks connected text for consistency, punctuation, spelling, grammar and clarity.
subtopics.worked_example: A passage can have individually correct sentences but inconsistent tense across sentences.
subtopics.pitfall: Editing is not rewriting every sentence.
subtopics.mastery: Edit systematically while preserving the intended message and voice.

subtopics.title: sentence construction
subtopics.teaching: Strong sentences have a clear subject, purposeful verb and relevant information.
subtopics.worked_example: 'The team practised after school because the final was near' combines a main clause and reason clause.
subtopics.pitfall: Longer sentences are not automatically better.
subtopics.mastery: Construct complete sentences and vary structure when useful.

subtopics.title: paragraph organization
subtopics.teaching: A coherent paragraph develops one controlling idea through a topic sentence, relevant support and an appropriate close or transition.
subtopics.worked_example: A paragraph about healthy sleep can state importance, give two benefits and connect them to daily habits.
subtopics.pitfall: Unrelated facts do not form a coherent paragraph.
subtopics.mastery: Arrange ideas logically and keep details connected to the main point.

subtopics.title: descriptive writing
subtopics.teaching: Descriptive writing uses precise sensory details and carefully selected vocabulary to create a focused impression.
subtopics.worked_example: Instead of 'The market was nice,' mention bright signs, spice smells and vendors' voices.
subtopics.pitfall: Many adjectives without relevant detail can remain vague.
subtopics.mastery: Use specific sensory evidence and precise nouns and verbs.

subtopics.title: narrative writing
subtopics.teaching: Narrative writing presents connected events and may include characters, setting, conflict, actions and resolution.
subtopics.worked_example: A story can establish a lost notebook, show the search and resolve the problem when it is found.
subtopics.pitfall: A sequence without connection or purpose feels like a list.
subtopics.mastery: Build coherent sequence with cause-and-effect and resolution.

subtopics.title: persuasive expression
subtopics.teaching: Persuasive writing states a position and supports it with reasons and evidence while considering the audience.
subtopics.worked_example: A recycling proposal can state the claim, give evidence, address convenience and propose action.
subtopics.pitfall: Persuasion is not repeated opinion or exaggerated language.
subtopics.mastery: State a clear claim and support it with relevant evidence and tone.

subtopics.title: character and setting
subtopics.teaching: Character refers to people or beings in a story; setting establishes when and where events occur and can influence behaviour.
subtopics.worked_example: A character crossing a flooded village faces different choices from one in a safe city, showing setting's effect.
subtopics.pitfall: Setting includes time, atmosphere and social conditions, not only location.
subtopics.mastery: Use textual details to explain character and setting relationships.

subtopics.title: plot conflict and resolution
subtopics.teaching: Plot is a sequence of connected events; conflict creates tension and resolution addresses the central problem.
subtopics.worked_example: Two friends disagree, face consequences and reconcile: interpersonal conflict drives later events.
subtopics.pitfall: The most dramatic event is not always the resolution.
subtopics.mastery: Trace the problem, turning points and outcome with evidence.

subtopics.title: theme and message
subtopics.teaching: Theme is a broader idea about life or experience developed by a text; a message communicates what the text suggests about it.
subtopics.worked_example: Repeated choices showing honesty despite difficulty may support a theme about integrity.
subtopics.pitfall: Theme should not be reduced to one plot detail.
subtopics.mastery: Infer theme from repeated patterns, choices, consequences and ending.

subtopics.title: figurative language
subtopics.teaching: Figurative language communicates beyond literal meaning through devices such as simile, metaphor, personification and hyperbole.
subtopics.worked_example: 'The classroom was a zoo' is metaphor for disorder or noise, not literal animals.
subtopics.pitfall: Literal interpretation can obscure intended effect.
subtopics.mastery: Identify the device and explain its contextual effect.

subtopics.title: poetry interpretation
subtopics.teaching: Poetry communicates through imagery, sound, rhythm, word choice, repetition, structure and figurative language.
subtopics.worked_example: Repeated darkness followed by morning may support an interpretation of difficulty followed by hope.
subtopics.pitfall: Interpretation must be grounded in the poem rather than personal association alone.
subtopics.mastery: Support interpretations with specific textual patterns.

subtopics.title: functional texts
subtopics.teaching: Functional texts serve practical purposes, including forms, schedules, emails, advertisements, menus and notices.
subtopics.worked_example: A timetable organizes times and locations so a reader can act quickly.
subtopics.pitfall: Reading a functional text like a story can hide key constraints.
subtopics.mastery: Extract purpose, key information, constraints and required action.

subtopics.title: instructions and notices
subtopics.teaching: Instructions specify procedures; notices communicate information, rules, changes or warnings.
subtopics.worked_example: A laboratory notice may state a safety rule while instructions provide the procedure steps.
subtopics.pitfall: A notice does not necessarily contain every task step.
subtopics.mastery: Identify sequence, conditions, prohibitions and actions.

subtopics.title: formal and informal language
subtopics.teaching: Formal language suits official, academic or professional contexts; informal language suits familiar conversation.
subtopics.worked_example: A request to a principal normally uses respectful formal register, unlike a message to a close friend.
subtopics.pitfall: Formal does not mean unnecessarily complicated.
subtopics.mastery: Match register to audience, purpose and situation.

subtopics.title: dialogue comprehension
subtopics.teaching: Dialogue reveals information through words, responses and implied intentions.
subtopics.worked_example: Repeatedly avoiding a direct question can imply discomfort even without stating it.
subtopics.pitfall: Literal words may not reveal full conversational intention.
subtopics.mastery: Track speakers, explicit information, implied meaning and attitude.

subtopics.title: information synthesis
subtopics.teaching: Synthesis combines relevant points from different parts or sources to form a supported conclusion.
subtopics.worked_example: A timetable gives event times and a notice gives eligibility; together they determine which event a student can attend.
subtopics.pitfall: Listing facts without explaining their relationship is not synthesis.
subtopics.mastery: Combine complementary evidence and state the supported conclusion.

subtopics.title: analogy
subtopics.teaching: An analogy compares relationships between pairs or groups of words; the relationship matters more than topic.
subtopics.worked_example: 'Bird : nest :: bee : hive' is animal to typical home.
subtopics.pitfall: Broad association is not the same as an equivalent relationship.
subtopics.mastery: Identify the precise first relationship before testing options.

subtopics.title: classification
subtopics.teaching: Classification groups items by a defining property or identifies an item that does not belong.
subtopics.worked_example: Apple, mango and banana can be fruits while carrot differs under that rule.
subtopics.pitfall: An item may fit multiple categories, so infer the intended rule from the set.
subtopics.mastery: State the rule and test every option against it.

subtopics.title: sentence completion
subtopics.teaching: Sentence completion depends on grammar, meaning, logical relationships and context.
subtopics.worked_example: 'The road was flooded, so the match was ___' supports 'cancelled' or 'postponed' depending on options.
subtopics.pitfall: Grammatical fit alone is insufficient if meaning conflicts.
subtopics.mastery: Use grammar and contextual logic together.

subtopics.title: word relationships
subtopics.teaching: Word relationships include part-whole, category-member, function, degree, cause-effect and opposites.
subtopics.worked_example: 'Page : book' is part-to-whole; 'teacher : school' can be person-to-workplace.
subtopics.pitfall: Common association does not guarantee the same relationship.
subtopics.mastery: Name the relationship and preserve its direction.

subtopics.title: verbal puzzles
subtopics.teaching: Verbal puzzles combine vocabulary, ordering, clues and logical constraints.
subtopics.worked_example: If A is before B and B before C, A-B-C follows even without a direct A-C clue.
subtopics.pitfall: Guessing before applying constraints causes errors.
subtopics.mastery: Extract every constraint and eliminate arrangements that violate any clue.

subtopics.title: language challenge strategy
subtopics.teaching: Identify whether an English challenge tests comprehension, vocabulary, grammar, editing, literature, communication, or reasoning before selecting a method.
subtopics.worked_example: For a sentence-correction question, first identify whether the issue concerns agreement, tense, word choice, punctuation, or structure.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: changing a sentence because it sounds unfamiliar without identifying a specific language rule.
subtopics.mastery: Classify the tested English skill and apply an evidence-based solving method.

subtopics.title: contextual meaning reasoning
subtopics.teaching: Infer word and phrase meaning from surrounding sentences, tone, grammar, and textual evidence rather than relying only on the most familiar definition.
subtopics.worked_example: A word with several meanings should be interpreted using the sentence and paragraph that surround it.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: selecting a dictionary meaning that conflicts with the passage context.
subtopics.mastery: Justify an interpretation using clear textual evidence.

subtopics.title: editing and error diagnosis
subtopics.teaching: Locate the first meaningful error in grammar, usage, punctuation, spelling, or sentence structure and explain the correction.
subtopics.worked_example: When a sentence contains a tense mismatch, identify the time reference and then correct the verb form consistently.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: correcting style preferences when the actual problem is grammatical or usage-based.
subtopics.mastery: Identify, explain, and correct an English language error accurately.

subtopics.title: integrated English challenges
subtopics.teaching: Combine reading, vocabulary, grammar, literary interpretation, writing, and verbal reasoning in unfamiliar formats.
subtopics.worked_example: A passage challenge may require identifying its main idea, interpreting a phrase, correcting an error, and selecting the strongest supporting sentence.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: solving each clue independently when the passage provides connected evidence.
subtopics.mastery: Combine multiple English skills to solve an integrated challenge.

subtopics.title: English championship round
subtopics.teaching: Practice timed mixed English challenges with careful reading, elimination, evidence checks, and final accuracy review.
subtopics.worked_example: Answer direct vocabulary and grammar questions first, then spend remaining time on longer comprehension and reasoning items.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: choosing an answer from a familiar keyword without rereading the relevant context.
subtopics.mastery: Complete a mixed English challenge accurately under time pressure and justify difficult answers from language evidence.
